DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION This paper demonstrates a method of visually identifying the offset of crop rows in agricultural fields using a learning algorithm to rapidly learn a model applicable to a specific field in a quick and practical way with minimal human input. Results demonstrate it is applicable to a wide variety of fields and crops, and is able to perform online guidance of a robot. Our method currently uses a one-off batch mode approach to training. In future work we would like to investigate methods of extending this method to performing continuous online learning to allow adaption to changing lighting and field conditions. One possible scheme we would like to investigate to allow online adaption is to temporarily stop the robot when our confidence measure falls below a threshold and to signal a remote operator to indicate the offset of one or more crop rows in a single image. This small amount of human input could then automatically generate many additional training examples that could be added to the original training set to retrain the model to also generalise t o this new field appearance. Output Filtering To improve tracking performance, we also apply spatial and temporal post processing to the output of the SVM. The predicted offset signal depicted in Figure 3.f is idealised and in practice we observe a noisier signal as shown in Figure 4.a. This makes locating the crop rows by at the local minima of this signal quite error prone. In order to more accurately locate the crop rows, we combine neighbouring offset predictions together by performing a template match of the predicted offset signal with the idealised template shown in Figure 4.b using a Sum of Squares Differences (SSD) similarity measure. The error output from this template matching produces a cleaner SSD Error signal shown in Figure 4.c. Note that the phase of this signal is opposite to the predicted offset, so crop rows are now located at the maxima of the SSD Error signal, and acceptable locations for our robot’s wheels (mid-way between the crop rows) are located at the minima. To further reduce noise, we also apply temporal filtering to the SSD Error signal with a simple complimentary filter, taking into account frame-to-frame offsets. The filtered SSD Error is used to estimate the position of the crop rows and desired wheel location. We calculate a steering signal by locating the minimum value in a region around the known offset of the wheel nearest to our camera (determined via prior calibration). G. Output Filtering To improve tracking performance, we also apply spatial and temporal post processing to the output of the SVM. The predicted offset signal depicted in Figure 3.f is idealised and in practice we observe a noisier signal as shown in Figure 4.a. This makes locating the crop rows by at the local minima of this signal quite error prone. In order to more accurately locate the crop rows, we combine neighbouring offset predictions together by performing a template match of the predicted offset signal with the idealised template shown in Figure 4.b using a Sum of Squares Differences (SSD) similarity measure. The error output from this template matching produces a cleaner SSD Error signal shown in Figure 4.c. Note that the phase of this signal is opposite to the predicted offset, so crop rows are now located at the maxima of the SSD Error signal, and acceptable locations for our robot’s wheels (mid-way between the crop rows) are located at the minima. To further reduce noise, we also apply temporal filtering to the SSD Error signal with a simple complimentary filter, taking into account frame-to-frame offsets. The filtered SSD Error is used to estimate the position of the crop rows and desired wheel location. We calculate a steering signal by locating the minimum value in a region around the known offset of the wheel nearest to our camera (determined via prior calibration). G. The methods above generally use a plant identification strategy that is tailored to a specific set of crop types or stage of development based on a prior assumption, for example that the crop is green or tall. However, the appearance and structure of fields change dramatically from crop to crop and throughout the year, and it can be difficult to select a crop row tracking method suitable to all the situations that an agricultural robot is likely to encounter. In previous work [1] we presented a vison-only crop row tracking algorithm that avoids segmenting crop from soil by tracking the parallel texture of the crop intensity. Figure 2 gives an overview of this method. We showed this method could reliably track the direction and relative offset of crops in varied and difficult conditions.
